Nguyen Hue was born in the year of Quy Dau 1753, the 13th year of the Canh Hung reign under King Le Hien Tong of the Later Le Dynasty. He was also known as Quang Binh,[11] Van Hue[12], or Ho Thom. Regarding the birth order of Nguyen Hue and Nguyen Lu among the brothers, documentary sources are inconsistent: The books Đại Nam thực lục chính biên, Đại Nam chính biên liệt truyện, and Tây Sơn thủy mạt khảo all agree on the order of the three Tay Son brothers, affirming that: "The eldest is Nhac, next is Lu, and then Hue"; The people of old Quy Nhon prefecture passed down that: Nguyen Nhac traded betel in his youth, so he was called Anh Hai Trau (Brother Two Betel), Nguyen Hue was also named Thom, so he was called Chu Ba Thom (Uncle Three Thom), and Nguyen Lu was called Thay Tu Lu (Master Four Lu).[a] According to letters from Western missionaries active in Dai Viet at that time, such as Labartette, Eyet, and Varen, Nguyen Hue was Nguyen Lu's younger brother. 3,	"Quang Trung (Chinese characters: 光中, 1753 – September 16, 1792), whose pre-coronation title was Bac Binh Vuong (北平王 - Prince of Northern Peace), birth name Ho Thom (胡𦹳), originally from Nghe An and later renamed Nguyen Hue (阮惠), was a Vietnamese politician and military leader. He was the 2nd emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated and passed the throne to him.

Nguyen Hue and his two brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes (Tây Sơn tam kiệt), were the leaders of the Tay Son uprising that ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war between the two feudal groups of Trinh in the north and Nguyen in the south, overthrowing these two groups along with the Later Le Dynasty, ending the division of Dang Trong (Inner Realm) and Dang Ngoai (Outer Realm) that lasted for 2 centuries. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. Nguyen Hue was born in the year of Quy Dau 1753, the 13th year of the Canh Hung reign under King Le Hien Tong of the Later Le Dynasty. He was also known as Quang Binh,[11] Van Hue[12], or Ho Thom. Later, local people often called him Duc Ong Binh (Lord Binh)[13] or Duc Ong Tam (Lord Eight).[8] According to Quang Trung anh hùng dân tộc (Quang Trung the National Hero), "Nguyen Hue had curly hair, textured skin, eyes that flashed like lightning, a voice as resonant as a bell, agile, strong, and brave." The book Tây Sơn lược also described Quang Trung's eyes: "at night, when sitting without a lamp, the light from his eyes illuminated the whole mat."

Regarding the birth order of Nguyen Hue and Nguyen Lu among the brothers, documentary sources are inconsistent: The books Đại Nam thực lục chính biên, Đại Nam chính biên liệt truyện, and Tây Sơn thủy mạt khảo all agree on the order of the three Tay Son brothers, affirming that: "The eldest is Nhac, next is Lu, and then Hue"; The people of old Quy Nhon prefecture passed down that: Nguyen Nhac traded betel in his youth, so he was called Anh Hai Trau (Brother Two Betel), Nguyen Hue was also named Thom, so he was called Chu Ba Thom (Uncle Three Thom), and Nguyen Lu was called Thay Tu Lu (Master Four Lu).[a] According to letters from Western missionaries active in Dai Viet at that time, such as Labartette, Eyet, and Varen, Nguyen Hue was Nguyen Lu's younger brother. Nguyen Lu was called Duc Ong Bay (Lord Seven) and Nguyen Hue was Duc Ong Tam (Lord Eight); Le Trong Ham in the book Minh đô sử argued that Ho Phi Phuc fathered "Nhac, Lu, then two daughters, and then Hue".

Growing up, he, Nguyen Nhac, and Nguyen Lu were sent to study both literature and martial arts with teacher Truong Van Hien. Truong Van Hien was a retainer of Truong Van Hanh, and Truong Van Hanh was the teacher of Nguyen Phuc Luan – Nguyen Anh's father. After Truong Van Hanh was harmed by the powerful courtier Truong Phuc Loan, Truong Van Hien fled to Binh Dinh. It was this teacher who discovered Nguyen Hue's abilities and advised the three brothers to rebel to build a great enterprise. Legend has it that the prophecy "Tay khoi nghia, Bac thu cong" (Rebel in the West, achieve success in the North) originated from Truong Van Hien.[14] Legend also has it that Nguyen Hue, Nguyen Nhac, and Nguyen Lu were all highly skilled in martial arts and were the founders of several Binh Dinh martial arts styles. Nguyen Hue created Yen Phi Quyen (Swallow Flight Form), Nguyen Lu created Hung Ke Quyen (Rooster Form), and all three Tay Son brothers created Doc Lu Thuong (Single Censer Spear). The three Tay Son heroes played a huge role in the formation and development of the Tay Son Binh Dinh martial arts sect, being the leaders who created and reformed empty-handed and weapon forms to teach the army in the early stages of the uprising.[15]"
4,	"Quang Trung (Chinese characters: 光中, 1753 – September 16, 1792), whose pre-coronation title was Bac Binh Vuong (北平王 - Prince of Northern Peace), birth name Ho Thom (胡𦹳), originally from Nghe An and later renamed Nguyen Hue (阮惠), was a Vietnamese politician and military leader. He was the 2nd emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated and passed the throne to him.

Nguyen Hue and his two brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes (Tây Sơn tam kiệt), were the leaders of the Tay Son uprising that ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war between the two feudal groups of Trinh in the north and Nguyen in the south, overthrowing these two groups along with the Later Le Dynasty, ending the division of Dang Trong (Inner Realm) and Dang Ngoai (Outer Realm) that lasted for 2 centuries. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. With a progressive vision, in just 3 years, he successively proposed many progressive reform plans in economics, culture, education, military,... to build the country and absorb modern science and technology from the West.[2] Regarding personnel, he issued an edict seeking talented people and heavily utilized many talents such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, Nguyen Huy Luong,... In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Regarding education, he improved the examination system in a practical direction, promulgated policies to encourage learning, encouraged the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions. Historians highly appreciate these reforms because they had a very progressive tendency, surpassing contemporary Asian countries, and could bring the country out of the stagnation that had lasted over 100 years under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system. Even much later (1822), overseas Chinese who lived in Hue under the Tay Son era still reminisced about Nguyen Hue's rule; they commented to a British merchant that Quang Trung ruled more mildly and fairly than the Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang)[3] (see details at progressive reforms of King Quang Trung).

The active life of Nguyen Hue made a decisive contribution to the cause of national reunification of the Tay Son dynasty[4]. After 20 years of continuous warfare and 3 years of ruling the country, when the country's situation began to show positive changes, Quang Trung died suddenly at the age of 39. After his death, the Tay Son Dynasty weakened rapidly. During the reign of the 6th Hung King, in Phu Dong village, Vu Ninh region, there was a wealthy family who had a son. By the time he was over three years old, he ate well and grew big but did not know how to speak or laugh. At a time when there was urgent news of danger in the country, the king sent envoys to find someone who could repel the enemy. On that day, the child suddenly spoke, telling his mother to invite the royal envoy in, and said: "Please grant me a sword and a horse, the king needs not worry about anything." The king granted him a sword and a horse; the child immediately rode the horse, brandished the sword, and charged forward with the royal army following behind, defeating the enemy troops at the foot of Vu Ninh mountain. The enemy troops turned their spears against each other, with many casualties; the survivors all bowed down, revered the child as a heavenly general, and immediately surrendered. The child rode his horse [4a] into the sky and departed. The king ordered the child's home garden to be renovated into a temple for annual sacrifices. Later, Ly Thai To granted him the title Xung Thien Than Vuong. (The temple is located next to Kien So pagoda, Phu Dong village).

During the reign of King Cheng of Zhou [1063-1026 BC], our country of Viet visited the Zhou dynasty for the first time (it is unclear during which Hung King's reign), claiming to be the Viet Thuong clan, and offered a white pheasant. The Duke of Zhou said: "If our political decrees do not reach them, a gentleman does not treat them as his subjects," and then ordered the construction of a south-pointing chariot to escort the envoys back to their country.

At the end of the Hung Vuong era, the king had a daughter named Mi Nuong, who was remarkably beautiful. Thuc Vuong heard of her and came to propose marriage. The king wanted to agree, but the Hung Hau advised against it: "They want to conquer our country and are only using marriage as an excuse." Because of this, Thuc Vuong harbored resentment. The king, wanting to find a worthy person to marry her to, told his subjects: "This daughter is of fairy descent; only someone with sufficient talent and virtue can be my son-in-law." At that time, two men arrived from outside and bowed in the courtyard to propose. The king found it strange; when asked, they replied that one was [4b] Son Tinh (Mountain Spirit) and the other was Thuy Tinh (Water Spirit), both from the great realm, who had heard the king had a divine daughter and made bold to come request her hand. The king said: "I have only one daughter, how can I have both of you as worthy sons-in-law?" He then set a condition that the next day, whoever brought sufficient betrothal gifts first would marry her. The two men obeyed, bowed in gratitude, and left. The next day, Son Tinh brought jewels, gold, silver, mountain birds, and forest beasts as gifts. The king kept his promise and married his daughter to him. Son Tinh took his wife to live on a high peak of Tan Vien mountain. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. With a progressive vision, in just 3 years, he successively proposed many progressive reform plans in economics, culture, education, military,... to build the country and absorb modern science and technology from the West.[2] Regarding personnel, he issued an edict seeking talented people and heavily utilized many talents such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, Nguyen Huy Luong,... In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Regarding education, he improved the examination system in a practical direction, promulgated policies to encourage learning, encouraged the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions. Historians highly appreciate these reforms because they had a very progressive tendency, surpassing contemporary Asian countries, and could bring the country out of the stagnation that had lasted over 100 years under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system. Even much later (1822), overseas Chinese who lived in Hue under the Tay Son era still reminisced about Nguyen Hue's rule; they commented to a British merchant that Quang Trung ruled more mildly and fairly than the Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang)[3] (see details at progressive reforms of King Quang Trung).

Kinh Duong Vuong
[1b] His taboo name was Loc Tuc, a descendant of the Than Nong clan.
Year of Nham Tuat, 17th year. In the past, De Minh, the third-generation descendant of Viem De of the Than Nong clan, fathered De Nghi. Later, during a tour of the South, De Minh reached Ngu Linh, married the daughter of Vu Tien, and fathered the king [Kinh Duong Vuong]. The king was a man of sagacious intelligence; De Minh loved him dearly and wanted him to succeed to the throne. The king persistently yielded to his older brother and dared not obey the command. De Minh then established De Nghi as the heir to rule the North, and enfeoffed the king as Kinh Duong Vuong to rule the South, calling it the kingdom of Xich Quy.
The king married the daughter of Dong Dinh Quan named Than Long, and fathered Lac Long Quan (Note: The Tang annals record: during the Kinh Duong period, there was a goat-herding woman who claimed to be the youngest daughter of Dong Dinh Quan; she married the second son of Kinh Xuyen but was abandoned, and wrote a letter asking Lieu Nghi to report this to Dong Dinh Quan. Thus, Kinh Xuyen and Dong Dinh had been allied by marriage for generations).

Lac Long Quan
[2a] His taboo name was Sung Lam, son of Kinh Duong Vuong.
The king married De Lai's daughter, Au Co, and fathered a hundred sons (legend has it she gave birth to a hundred eggs), who are the ancestors of the Bach Viet. One day, the king said to Au Co: "I am of the dragon race, you are of the fairy race; water and fire are incompatible, it is truly difficult for us to be together." question: Who were the three brothers of the Tay Son movement?
answer:
The **Tay Son movement** (1771–1802) was a pivotal force in Vietnamese history, led by three brothers who played central roles in unifying the country and challenging the Trinh and Nguyen dynasties. These brothers were **Nguyen Nhac** (the eldest), **Nguyen Lu** (the middle brother), and **Nguyen Hue** (the youngest, later known as **Quang Trung**). Their collaboration and leadership were instrumental in the movement’s rise and eventual success. Below is a summary of their roles, birth order, and historical context.

---

### **Birth Order and Titles**  
The birth order of the three brothers is a subject of historical debate, with conflicting accounts in primary sources.  
- **According to the *Đại Nam thực lục chính biên* and *Tây Sơn thủy mạt khảo***, the order is **Nguyen Nhac (eldest)**, **Nguyen Lu (second)**, and **Nguyen Hue (youngest)**.  
- **Local traditions in Quy Nhon** suggest a different order, with Nguyen Nhac referred to as *Anh Hai Trau* (Brother Two Betel) and Nguyen Hue as *Chu Ba Thom* (Uncle Three Thom), implying a younger position for Nguyen Hue.  
- **Western missionaries** like Labartette and Varen noted that Nguyen Hue was the younger brother of Nguyen Lu, with Nguyen Lu called *Duc Ong Bay* (Lord Seven) and Nguyen Hue *Duc Ong Tam* (Lord Eight).  

Despite these discrepancies, **Nguyen Hue** (Quang Trung) is most prominently associated with the movement’s military and political success, while **Nguyen Nhac** and **Nguyen Lu** played critical roles in its early organization and governance.

---

### **Early Lives and Education**  
The three brothers were raised in a family that emphasized both scholarly and martial pursuits. They studied under **Truong Van Hien**, a former retainer of **Truong Van Hanh**, who was himself a teacher to **Nguyen Phuc Luan** (father of the later Nguyen dynasty). Truong Van Hien is credited with inspiring the brothers to rebel against the corrupt court and establish the Tay Son movement.  

- **Prophecy and Martial Arts**: The legend of the prophecy *"Tay khoi nghia, Bac thu cong"* (Rebel in the West, achieve success in the North) is attributed to Truong Van Hien. The brothers were also said to have mastered martial arts, founding styles such as **Yen Phi Quyen** (Nguyen Hue), **Hung Ke Quyen** (Nguyen Lu), and **Doc Lu Thuong** (a combined weapon form). These styles became foundational to the **Tay Son Binh Dinh martial arts sect**, which trained soldiers during the uprising.  

---

### **Leadership and Legacy**  
- **Nguyen Hue (Quang Trung)**: As the youngest brother, Nguyen Hue became the movement’s most celebrated leader. His military genius, including the decisive **Battle of Chi Lang** (1789), led to the unification of Vietnam under Tay Son rule. His leadership style, characterized by strategic brilliance and charisma, earned him titles like *Duc Ong Binh* (Lord Binh) and *Duc Ong Tam* (Lord Eight).  
- **Nguyen Nhac**: The eldest brother, Nguyen Nhac, was the first to lead the rebellion, establishing the Tay Son movement’s base in Binh Dinh. He focused on consolidating power in the south before passing leadership to Nguyen Hue.  
- **Nguyen Lu**: The middle brother, Nguyen Lu, played a key role in administrative and military affairs, ensuring the movement’s stability. His contributions to the formation of the Tay Son Binh Dinh martial arts sect were significant.  

The brothers’ collaboration and distinct roles exemplify the synergy of leadership, strategy, and cultural heritage that defined the Tay Son movement. Their legacy endures as a symbol of Vietnamese resilience and unity against external and internal threats.

His death marked the end of the Tay Son Dynasty's golden era, as his military and political achievements were unparalleled, and his passing left a power vacuum that the dynasty could not sustain.

After Quang Trung's death, the Tay Son Dynasty faced rapid decline. His brothers, **Nguyen Nhac** (the eldest) and **Nguyen Lu** (the second), were left to govern, but they lacked the charisma and strategic acumen of their younger brother. Internal strife and factionalism eroded the dynasty's cohesion. Meanwhile, **Nguyen Anh**, the son of **Nguyen Phuc Luan** (a former retainer of the Tay Son), capitalized on the chaos. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. The descendant of the Than Nong clan, De Minh, married the daughter of Vu Tien and fathered Kinh Duong Vuong, who is the founding ancestor of the Bach Viet. The king married the daughter of Than Long and fathered Lac Long Quan; Lac Long Quan married the daughter of De Lai and had the auspicious blessing of fathering a hundred sons. Is that not what laid the foundation for our Viet nation's enterprise? Examining the Tongjian Waiji (Comprehensive Mirror, Outer Annals), it states: De Lai was the son of De Nghi; according to that record, Kinh Duong Vuong was the biological younger brother of De Nghi, yet they intermarried; perhaps it was because that era was still primitive and rites and music had not yet been established?

Hung Vuong
[3a] The son of Lac Long Quan (taboo name unknown), established the capital in Phong Chau (now Bach Hac district).
Upon ascending the throne, Hung Vuong set the national name as Van Lang (this country bordered the South Sea to the east, Ba Thuc to the west, Dong Dinh lake to the north, and Ho Ton - which is Champa, now Quang Nam - to the south). He divided the country into 15 administrative regions: Giao Chi, Chu Dien, Vu Ninh, Phuc Loc, Viet Thuong, Ninh Hai, Duong Tuyen, Luc Hai, Vu Dinh, Hoai Hoan, Cuu Chan, Binh Van, Tan Hung, Cuu Duc; all were vassal lands of Hung Vuong; while the region called Van Lang was where the king established the capital. He appointed civil generals called Lac Hau, and military generals called Lac Tuong. The king's sons were called Quan Lang, and daughters were called Mi Nuong. Officials in charge of affairs were called Bo Chinh; their hereditary succession from father to son was called phu dao. Kings of all generations were called Hung Vuong. At that time, the people living in the forests and mountains saw that the rivers and streams had shrimp and fish, so they invited each other to catch fish for food, but were often harmed by water monsters (thuong luong). [3b] They came to report this to the king. The king said: "The barbarians in the mountains are different from aquatic species; those aquatic species favor their own kind and hate other species, which is why you are harmed by them." The king then told everyone to use ink to tattoo images of water monsters on their bodies. From then on, the water monsters saw them and no longer bit or harmed them. The tattooing custom of the Bach Viet people probably started from there.

### Artists and Album Information  
**"Love the Way You Lie"** is a collaborative song featuring **Eminem** and **Rihanna**. The track appears on Eminem's seventh studio album, **Recovery**, which was released on **June 21, 2010**.  

### Context and Release  
The song was initially released as a **radio single** in 2010 and later distributed as a **CD** in the UK on **August 9, 2010**, with **Interscope Records** handling its release in Germany on **August 20, 2010**. It is widely regarded as one of the standout tracks from *Recovery*, praised for its emotional depth and the dynamic interplay between Eminem's introspective lyrics and Rihanna's haunting vocal delivery.  

### Thematic Significance  
The song explores themes of **domestic violence** and a **mutually destructive relationship**, with Eminem reflecting on his past struggles, including references to his ex-partner **Kim Kardashian** and the 2009 incident involving **Chris Brown** and Rihanna. Rihanna's contribution is highlighted as a poignant commentary on the cyclical nature of abuse, with her lyrics emphasizing the emotional toll of such relationships.  

### Production Details  
The track was recorded and mixed by **Mike Strange** at **Effigy Studios** in Ferndale, Michigan, with additional input from **Alex da Kid** for mastering. Rihanna's vocals were recorded at **Sun Studios** in Dublin, Ireland, under the engineering of **Marcos Tovar**. The song's production blends **hip hop** and **pop** elements, featuring piano, electric guitar, and orchestral arrangements that enhance its emotional resonance.  

This collaboration marked a significant moment in both artists' careers, blending Eminem's signature rap style with Rihanna's vocal artistry to create a powerful and introspective piece.

Skylar Grey’s involvement with "Love the Way You Lie" began in late 2009 when she was staying at the Artula Retreat in Bandon, Oregon. During this time, she focused on writing songs, including the track that would eventually become "Love the Way You Lie." Her creative process was influenced by her own experiences, as she later described feeling trapped in an abusive relationship with the music industry. In early 2010, Grey visited her Universal Music publisher, Jennifer Blakeman, in New York City to seek guidance on presenting her work. Blakeman recommended she collaborate with producer Alex da Kid, who had a reputation for crafting emotionally resonant tracks.  

Da Kid sent Grey a backing track, which he had developed by layering electronic drum rhythms and live instrumentation. The track’s melody and theme of abusive relationships resonated with Grey, inspiring her to spontaneously write lyrics. She completed the chorus in just fifteen minutes, a testament to the song’s immediate emotional impact. Grey recorded her vocals for a demo, which she shared with da Kid. This collaboration marked the initial phase of the song’s creation, blending Grey’s lyrical vision with da Kid’s production expertise.

Following the demo, Alex da Kid shared some of his backing tracks with Rigo Morales, a senior director at Shady Records. Morales, who was seeking a fresh musical direction for Eminem’s upcoming album *Recovery*, was impressed by the tracks’ emotional depth and unique sound. Eminem was particularly drawn to the track’s theme of toxic relationships, a subject he had explored in past work like "Kim" (2000) and "'97 Bonnie & Clyde" (1998).

The song "Love the Way You Lie" by Eminem and Rihanna draws on the personal experiences of both artists, particularly their histories with abusive relationships. These experiences are woven into the song’s narrative of mutual violence and emotional turmoil, reflecting real-life struggles that shaped its creation. Below is a breakdown of the relevant details:

---

### **Eminem’s Experiences with Kim Scott**  
Eminem’s verses in the song reference his tumultuous relationship with his ex-wife, Kim Scott. The lyrics allude to his past verbal and emotional abuse, as well as the cyclical nature of their toxic dynamic. For instance, the line *"I laid hands on her. I'll never stoop so low again / I guess I don't know my own strength"* directly addresses his admission of physical violence, which he had previously hinted at in earlier works like *"Kim"* (2000) and *"97 Bonnie & Clyde"* (1998). These songs depicted his fantasies of murdering Scott, reflecting a pattern of control and resentment. Their relationship ended in 2001, and they remarried before divorcing again in 2003. The song’s exploration of regret and self-reflection mirrors Eminem’s own struggles with accountability and the aftermath of their relationship.

---

### **Rihanna’s Experience with Chris Brown**  
Rihanna’s perspective on the song is deeply tied to her 2009 relationship with R&B singer Chris Brown, which ended after he was convicted of felony assault for beating her. The song’s lyrics, such as *"If she ever tries to fuckin' leave again, I'ma tie her to the bed and set this house on fire,"* are interpreted as a reference to this incident. Rihanna has stated that the song’s theme of domestic violence resonated with her because she felt many people lacked understanding of the issue. Her collaboration with Eminem allowed her to channel her experiences into the track, emphasizing the cyclical nature of abuse and the emotional toll it takes on both parties. The song’s title itself, *"Love the Way You Lie,"* encapsulates the paradox of loving someone while enduring their harmful behavior—a dynamic Rihanna described as a "cycle of domestic violence."

---

### **Shared Themes and Collaborative Influence**  
Both artists’ experiences with abusive relationships influenced the song’s creation. Eminem, who had previously explored themes of toxic love and violence in his music, saw in Rihanna’s perspective a mirror of his own struggles. The song’s structure—alternating between Rihanna’s melodic, vulnerable verses and Eminem’s raw, confrontational raps—reflects the duality of their experiences: Rihanna’s portrayal of enduring pain and Eminem’s acknowledgment of his role in perpetuating it. The collaboration was also driven by their mutual understanding of the topic, as Rihanna noted that the song "broke down the cycle of domestic violence" by giving voice to a subject often overlooked. This shared history of abuse and reconciliation is central to the song’s emotional weight and its impact as a commentary on toxic relationships.

The development of "Love the Way You Lie" began with the backing track and hook melody, which was created by British hip hop producer Alex da Kid.[2] When making a track, he explained that he spends hours making loops and produces an electronic drum rhythm before adding live instrumentation. The drums are sampled from live recordings he saved.[3] Alex da Kid recorded an acoustic guitar for the verses with a Neumann U 87 microphone and an Avid Mbox audio interface. He told Sound on Sound magazine that this song had given him an opportunity to reintroduce live guitar in hip hop music.[3] During the session, he used Waves RVerb and REQ equalization on his main kick track and a MaxxBass plug-in on two others.[2]

Writing began in late 2009, when singer Skylar Grey resided at the Artula Retreat in Bandon, Oregon,[4] and wrote songs.[5] Later, in New York City, she visited her Universal Music publisher, Jennifer Blakeman, to seek help presenting her work;[5][6] Blakeman suggested she collaborate with Alex da Kid.[5] The producer emailed Grey his track, which suggested a theme of abusive romantic relationships to her as she spontaneously sang lyrics to the melody.[7] She told the Los Angeles Times that she was in an abusive relationship with the music industry: "I love it so much, and I give it all that I have, yet it beats me down."[8] This idea inspired her writing,[8] a process she found came naturally, as if she were creating an alternative pop song for herself.[9] She wrote the chorus to "Love the Way You Lie" in fifteen minutes and recorded vocals for Alex da Kid's demo.[5][10]

question: Arrange the main events in the song's development in chronological order.
answer:
# Chronological Development of the Tay Son Uprising and Quang Trung's Reign

## Early Origins and Family Background

The Tay Son uprising began with the rise of the Tay Son brothers—Nguyen Nhac, Nguyen Lu, and Nguyen Hue. According to historical records, Nguyen Hue was the youngest of the three, with Nguyen Nhac as the eldest and Nguyen Lu as the middle brother. Their family origins are traced back to the Ho clan in Huong Cai village, Hung Nguyen district, Nghe An province. The family originally bore the surname Ho, descended from Ho Quy Ly, and followed Lord Nguyen to settle in the South when he crossed the Thay Wall in 1655. Over time, the family changed their surname to Nguyen, following the mother's lineage, due to their marriage to a wealthy merchant's daughter, Nguyen Thi.

Nguyen Hue's father, Ho Phi Phuc, moved the family to Kien Thanh hamlet, where they engaged in the betel trade. This trade led to the family's prosperity and eventual settlement in the region. The family's transition from the Ho to the Nguyen surname marked a significant shift in their social and political status.

## Education and Early Rebellion

Nguyen Hue, along with his brothers, was sent to study both literature and martial arts under the teacher Truong Van Hien. This teacher, a former retainer of Truong Van Hanh, who was the mentor of Nguyen Phuc Luan (Nguyen Anh's father), played a crucial role in shaping the brothers' future. After Truong Van Hanh was harmed by the powerful courtier Truong Phuc Loan, Truong Van Hien fled to Binh Dinh, where he discovered Nguyen Hue's abilities and advised the three brothers to rebel against the existing feudal order.

The prophecy "Tay khoi nghia, Bac thu cong" (Rebel in the West, achieve success in the North) is believed to have originated from Truong Van Hien, marking the beginning of the Tay Son uprising. The brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes, were highly skilled in martial arts and are credited with the creation of several Binh Dinh martial arts styles, including Yen Phi Quyen (Swallow Flight Form), Hung Ke Quyen (Rooster Form), and Doc Lu Thuong (Single Censer Spear).

## Rise to Power and the End of the Trinh–Nguyen Civil War

The Tay Son uprising, led by the three brothers, culminated in the end of the Trinh–Nguyen civil war, which had divided Vietnam for over two centuries. The uprising successfully overthrew both the Trinh in the north and the Nguyen in the south, as well as the Later Le Dynasty. This marked the unification of Vietnam under the Tay Son Dynasty.

Nguyen Hue, the youngest brother, became the second emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated in favor of him. His reign, known as the Quang Trung era, was characterized by a series of progressive reforms and military campaigns.

## Military Campaigns and National Reunification

Quang Trung, as he was known after his coronation, was a brilliant military leader who personally commanded troops from the age of 18. Over 20 years of continuous warfare, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one. His military campaigns were instrumental in the national reunification of Vietnam, as he defeated the invasions of Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north.

## Progressive Reforms and Governance

As emperor, Quang Trung implemented a series of progressive reforms that had a significant impact on Vietnam's development. These reforms included economic, cultural, educational, and military changes. He reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. In education, he improved the examination system, promoted the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions.

Quang Trung also issued an edict seeking talented individuals and heavily utilized many skilled officials such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, and Nguyen Huy Luong. His reforms were highly regarded by historians for their progressive nature, surpassing contemporary Asian countries and helping to bring Vietnam out of the stagnation of the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system.

## Death and Legacy

Quang Trung died suddenly at the age of 39, marking the end of his reign. His death led to the rapid decline of the Tay Son Dynasty, as his successor, Quang Toan, was too young to lead effectively. The royal court fell into internal conflict, and the dynasty failed to continue resisting the Nguyen Anh forces.

Despite his early death, Quang Trung's legacy endured. He is listed by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as one of Vietnam's 14 typical national heroes. Many schools and streets in Vietnam are named after him, reflecting his lasting impact on Vietnamese history and culture.

Skylar Grey wrote and recorded a demo of the song alongside producer Alex da Kid. Eminem wrote the verses and chose Rihanna to sing the chorus, resulting in a collaboration influenced by their past experiences in difficult relationships. Recording sessions were held in Ferndale, Michigan, and Dublin, Ireland. Backed by guitar, piano and violin, the track is a midtempo hip-hop ballad with a pop refrain, sung by Rihanna, and describes two lovers who refuse to separate despite being in an abusive relationship.

Eminem promoted the single with performances at the 2010 Electronic Entertainment Expo, the MTV Video Music Awards and festivals. The music video, directed by Joseph Kahn, stars Dominic Monaghan and Megan Fox as lovers in a violent relationship and shows Eminem and Rihanna in front of a burning house. The video met with a mixed reception due to scenes of domestic violence. Reporters suggested that the song and its accompanying video were influenced by Eminem's and Rihanna's abusive relationships with their respective ex-lovers, Kim Scott and Chris Brown.

Critics listed "Love the Way You Lie" among the best tracks of 2010 and of Eminem's career. The song won many awards and received five Grammy nominations. It is Eminem's best-selling single and ranked number one on several record charts, including the US Billboard Hot 100 for seven weeks. The single sold over 12 million copies in the US and 1.5 million in the UK. Musical acts such as Cher Lloyd and the Band Perry have performed cover versions. Rihanna has said that the theme of domestic violence, a topic on which she claims many people do not have insight, is what makes the song impactful. She later recorded with him again on "Love the Way You Lie (Part II)", narrated mostly from her perspective. "Love the Way You Lie" peaked at number one in 22 countries.

The development of "Love the Way You Lie" began with the backing track and hook melody, which was created by British hip hop producer Alex da Kid.[2] When making a track, he explained that he spends hours making loops and produces an electronic drum rhythm before adding live instrumentation. The drums are sampled from live recordings he saved.[3] Alex da Kid recorded an acoustic guitar for the verses with a Neumann U 87 microphone and an Avid Mbox audio interface. He told Sound on Sound magazine that this song had given him an opportunity to reintroduce live guitar in hip hop music.[3] During the session, he used Waves RVerb and REQ equalization on his main kick track and a MaxxBass plug-in on two others.[2]

Writing began in late 2009, when singer Skylar Grey resided at the Artula Retreat in Bandon, Oregon,[4] and wrote songs.[5] Later, in New York City, she visited her Universal Music publisher, Jennifer Blakeman, to seek help presenting her work;[5][6] Blakeman suggested she collaborate with Alex da Kid.[5] The producer emailed Grey his track, which suggested a theme of abusive romantic relationships to her as she spontaneously sang lyrics to the melody.[7] She told the Los Angeles Times that she was in an abusive relationship with the music industry: "I love it so much, and I give it all that I have, yet it beats me down."[8] This idea inspired her writing,[8] a process she found came naturally, as if she were creating an alternative pop song for herself.[9] She wrote the chorus to "Love the Way You Lie" in fifteen minutes and recorded vocals for Alex da Kid's demo.[5][10]

In early 2010, Alex da Kid offered Shady Records senior director Rigo Morales some backing tracks.[11] Morales enjoyed the tracks and sent them to Eminem, who was seeking a different musical approach for his next album.[11] Impressed with Alex da Kid's work, Eminem asked for more tracks and subsequently heard "Love the Way You Lie". He chose it and told his manager Paul Rosenberg he wanted to collaborate with the Barbadian singer Rihanna.[11] Eminem told Skyrock, "It's one of those tracks that I felt like only she could pull it off."[12] Rosenberg sent the track to Rihanna, who accepted Eminem's request "at the last moment."[11] Eminem wrote the rapped verses to the song.[10]

Rihanna has also said she joined the collaboration because she could relate to the theme of the song, as she and Eminem had been in difficult relationships on "different ends of the table".[13] Eminem had released the songs "'97 Bonnie & Clyde" (1998) and "Kim" (2000), in which he fantasizes, respectively, about murdering and verbally abusing his then-wife Kim Scott.[14] They had divorced in 2001 and again in 2006 after a remarriage.[15] In February 2009, Rihanna's relationship with the R&B singer Chris Brown had ended following his felony assault on her.[16] Rihanna described "Love the Way You Lie" as unique, realistic and deep, saying that it "broke down the cycle of domestic violence" because few people had insight on the topic.[13][17][18]

The transformation of *"Love the Way You Lie"* from its initial demo to the final release involved a collaborative effort between multiple key figures in music production. **Mike Strange**, who recorded and mixed Eminem's vocals at Effigy Studios in Ferndale, Michigan, played a central role. He handled the vocal editing, using tools like D-Verb and Extra Long Delay plugins, and focused on board compression and console equalization to refine the track. Strange emphasized that the core elements of the song were already in place, and his task was to "match and improve" the demo sent by **Alex da Kid**, who later joined the project to assist with mixing and mastering.  

Alex da Kid’s contribution was pivotal in shaping the final sound. While he initially wanted to replace the acoustic guitar on the demo, Eminem opted to retain it, preserving the song’s original character. Strange noted that da Kid’s involvement was about refining the track to align with the demo’s vision. Additionally, **Joe Strange**, Mike’s brother, served as the engineer for the track, ensuring technical precision during the production process.  

For Rihanna’s vocals, **Marcos Tovar** engineered the sessions at Sun Studios in Dublin, Ireland, while **Makeba Riddick** provided additional vocal production. Tovar and Riddick worked to balance Rihanna’s vocal performance with the instrumental arrangement, ensuring her emotional delivery complemented the track’s mood. Together, these collaborators—Strange, da Kid, Tovar, Riddick, and Joe Strange—bridged the gap between the demo and the final release, refining both the sonic and emotional elements of the song.

Detroit musician Luis Resto has contributed to the arrangement on many of Eminem's songs, but did not do so for "Love the Way You Lie". Rihanna's recording sessions took place at Sun Studios in Dublin, Ireland, and were engineered by Marcos Tovar. The R&B songwriter Makeba Riddick provided additional vocal production.[19] Strange used equalization, compression and reverberation but left the vocal balance. 3,	"Quang Trung (Chinese characters: 光中, 1753 – September 16, 1792), whose pre-coronation title was Bac Binh Vuong (北平王 - Prince of Northern Peace), birth name Ho Thom (胡𦹳), originally from Nghe An and later renamed Nguyen Hue (阮惠), was a Vietnamese politician and military leader. He was the 2nd emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated and passed the throne to him.

Nguyen Hue and his two brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes (Tây Sơn tam kiệt), were the leaders of the Tay Son uprising that ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war between the two feudal groups of Trinh in the north and Nguyen in the south, overthrowing these two groups along with the Later Le Dynasty, ending the division of Dang Trong (Inner Realm) and Dang Ngoai (Outer Realm) that lasted for 2 centuries. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. With a progressive vision, in just 3 years, he successively proposed many progressive reform plans in economics, culture, education, military,... to build the country and absorb modern science and technology from the West.[2] Regarding personnel, he issued an edict seeking talented people and heavily utilized many talents such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, Nguyen Huy Luong,... In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Regarding education, he improved the examination system in a practical direction, promulgated policies to encourage learning, encouraged the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions. Historians highly appreciate these reforms because they had a very progressive tendency, surpassing contemporary Asian countries, and could bring the country out of the stagnation that had lasted over 100 years under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system. Even much later (1822), overseas Chinese who lived in Hue under the Tay Son era still reminisced about Nguyen Hue's rule; they commented to a British merchant that Quang Trung ruled more mildly and fairly than the Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang)[3] (see details at progressive reforms of King Quang Trung).

The active life of Nguyen Hue made a decisive contribution to the cause of national reunification of the Tay Son dynasty[4]. After 20 years of continuous warfare and 3 years of ruling the country, when the country's situation began to show positive changes, Quang Trung died suddenly at the age of 39. After his death, the Tay Son Dynasty weakened rapidly. His successor, Quang Toan, was still too young (9 years old) to lead Dai Viet; the royal court fell into internal conflict and failed to continue resisting Nguyen Anh.

Nguyen Hue is listed by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as one of the 14 typical national heroes of Vietnam.[5] Many schools and streets in localities are named Quang Trung and Nguyen Hue.

Nguyen Hue was born in the year of Quy Dau 1753, the 13th year of the Canh Hung reign under King Le Hien Tong of the Later Le Dynasty. He was also known as Quang Binh,[11] Van Hue[12], or Ho Thom. Later, local people often called him Duc Ong Binh (Lord Binh)[13] or Duc Ong Tam (Lord Eight).[8] According to Quang Trung anh hùng dân tộc (Quang Trung the National Hero), "Nguyen Hue had curly hair, textured skin, eyes that flashed like lightning, a voice as resonant as a bell, agile, strong, and brave." The book Tây Sơn lược also described Quang Trung's eyes: "at night, when sitting without a lamp, the light from his eyes illuminated the whole mat."

Regarding the birth order of Nguyen Hue and Nguyen Lu among the brothers, documentary sources are inconsistent: The books Đại Nam thực lục chính biên, Đại Nam chính biên liệt truyện, and Tây Sơn thủy mạt khảo all agree on the order of the three Tay Son brothers, affirming that: "The eldest is Nhac, next is Lu, and then Hue"; The people of old Quy Nhon prefecture passed down that: Nguyen Nhac traded betel in his youth, so he was called Anh Hai Trau (Brother Two Betel), Nguyen Hue was also named Thom, so he was called Chu Ba Thom (Uncle Three Thom), and Nguyen Lu was called Thay Tu Lu (Master Four Lu).[a] According to letters from Western missionaries active in Dai Viet at that time, such as Labartette, Eyet, and Varen, Nguyen Hue was Nguyen Lu's younger brother. 1,	"Hong Bang Dynasty Era

Kinh Duong Vuong
[1b] His taboo name was Loc Tuc, a descendant of the Than Nong clan.
Year of Nham Tuat, 17th year. In the past, De Minh, the third-generation descendant of Viem De of the Than Nong clan, fathered De Nghi. Later, during a tour of the South, De Minh reached Ngu Linh, married the daughter of Vu Tien, and fathered the king [Kinh Duong Vuong]. The king was a man of sagacious intelligence; De Minh loved him dearly and wanted him to succeed to the throne. The king persistently yielded to his older brother and dared not obey the command. De Minh then established De Nghi as the heir to rule the North, and enfeoffed the king as Kinh Duong Vuong to rule the South, calling it the kingdom of Xich Quy.
The king married the daughter of Dong Dinh Quan named Than Long, and fathered Lac Long Quan (Note: The Tang annals record: during the Kinh Duong period, there was a goat-herding woman who claimed to be the youngest daughter of Dong Dinh Quan; she married the second son of Kinh Xuyen but was abandoned, and wrote a letter asking Lieu Nghi to report this to Dong Dinh Quan. Thus, Kinh Xuyen and Dong Dinh had been allied by marriage for generations).

Lac Long Quan
[2a] His taboo name was Sung Lam, son of Kinh Duong Vuong.
The king married De Lai's daughter, Au Co, and fathered a hundred sons (legend has it she gave birth to a hundred eggs), who are the ancestors of the Bach Viet. One day, the king said to Au Co: "I am of the dragon race, you are of the fairy race; water and fire are incompatible, it is truly difficult for us to be together." They then bid each other farewell, dividing 50 children to follow their mother to the mountains, and 50 children to follow their father to the South (some versions record to the South Sea), and enfeoffed the eldest son as Hung Vuong to succeed the throne.
Historian Ngo Si Lien said: When heaven and earth were first formed, there was a being created from vital energy, which was the Pan Gu clan. From the manifestation of energy came the manifestation of physical forms; nothing exists outside the two energies of yin and yang. The I Ching says: "Heaven and earth intermingle, all things are transformed and purified; male and female unite their essences, all things are born." Therefore, there is husband and wife first, then father and son, and after father and son comes ruler and subject. [2b] However, the birth of sages and worthies is always extraordinary, which is due to the mandate of heaven. Swallowing a dark bird's egg to give birth to the Shang dynasty, stepping on a giant's footprint to establish the Zhou dynasty, are all recorded facts of this nature. The descendant of the Than Nong clan, De Minh, married the daughter of Vu Tien and fathered Kinh Duong Vuong, who is the founding ancestor of the Bach Viet. The king married the daughter of Than Long and fathered Lac Long Quan; Lac Long Quan married the daughter of De Lai and had the auspicious blessing of fathering a hundred sons. Is that not what laid the foundation for our Viet nation's enterprise? Examining the Tongjian Waiji (Comprehensive Mirror, Outer Annals), it states: De Lai was the son of De Nghi; according to that record, Kinh Duong Vuong was the biological younger brother of De Nghi, yet they intermarried; perhaps it was because that era was still primitive and rites and music had not yet been established?

Hung Vuong
[3a] The son of Lac Long Quan (taboo name unknown), established the capital in Phong Chau (now Bach Hac district).
Upon ascending the throne, Hung Vuong set the national name as Van Lang (this country bordered the South Sea to the east, Ba Thuc to the west, Dong Dinh lake to the north, and Ho Ton - which is Champa, now Quang Nam - to the south). He divided the country into 15 administrative regions: Giao Chi, Chu Dien, Vu Ninh, Phuc Loc, Viet Thuong, Ninh Hai, Duong Tuyen, Luc Hai, Vu Dinh, Hoai Hoan, Cuu Chan, Binh Van, Tan Hung, Cuu Duc; all were vassal lands of Hung Vuong; while the region called Van Lang was where the king established the capital. He appointed civil generals called Lac Hau, and military generals called Lac Tuong. The king's sons were called Quan Lang, and daughters were called Mi Nuong. Officials in charge of affairs were called Bo Chinh; their hereditary succession from father to son was called phu dao. Kings of all generations were called Hung Vuong. At that time, the people living in the forests and mountains saw that the rivers and streams had shrimp and fish, so they invited each other to catch fish for food, but were often harmed by water monsters (thuong luong). [3b] They came to report this to the king. The king said: "The barbarians in the mountains are different from aquatic species; those aquatic species favor their own kind and hate other species, which is why you are harmed by them." The king then told everyone to use ink to tattoo images of water monsters on their bodies. From then on, the water monsters saw them and no longer bit or harmed them. The tattooing custom of the Bach Viet people probably started from there.

By the time he was over three years old, he ate well and grew big but did not know how to speak or laugh. At a time when there was urgent news of danger in the country, the king sent envoys to find someone who could repel the enemy. On that day, the child suddenly spoke, telling his mother to invite the royal envoy in, and said: "Please grant me a sword and a horse, the king needs not worry about anything." The king granted him a sword and a horse; the child immediately rode the horse, brandished the sword, and charged forward with the royal army following behind, defeating the enemy troops at the foot of Vu Ninh mountain. The enemy troops turned their spears against each other, with many casualties; the survivors all bowed down, revered the child as a heavenly general, and immediately surrendered. The child rode his horse [4a] into the sky and departed. The king ordered the child's home garden to be renovated into a temple for annual sacrifices. Later, Ly Thai To granted him the title Xung Thien Than Vuong. (The temple is located next to Kien So pagoda, Phu Dong village).

During the reign of King Cheng of Zhou [1063-1026 BC], our country of Viet visited the Zhou dynasty for the first time (it is unclear during which Hung King's reign), claiming to be the Viet Thuong clan, and offered a white pheasant. The Duke of Zhou said: "If our political decrees do not reach them, a gentleman does not treat them as his subjects," and then ordered the construction of a south-pointing chariot to escort the envoys back to their country.

At the end of the Hung Vuong era, the king had a daughter named Mi Nuong, who was remarkably beautiful. Thuc Vuong heard of her and came to propose marriage. The king wanted to agree, but the Hung Hau advised against it: "They want to conquer our country and are only using marriage as an excuse." Because of this, Thuc Vuong harbored resentment. The king, wanting to find a worthy person to marry her to, told his subjects: "This daughter is of fairy descent; only someone with sufficient talent and virtue can be my son-in-law." At that time, two men arrived from outside and bowed in the courtyard to propose. The king found it strange; when asked, they replied that one was [4b] Son Tinh (Mountain Spirit) and the other was Thuy Tinh (Water Spirit), both from the great realm, who had heard the king had a divine daughter and made bold to come request her hand. The king said: "I have only one daughter, how can I have both of you as worthy sons-in-law?" He then set a condition that the next day, whoever brought sufficient betrothal gifts first would marry her. The two men obeyed, bowed in gratitude, and left. The next day, Son Tinh brought jewels, gold, silver, mountain birds, and forest beasts as gifts. The king kept his promise and married his daughter to him. Son Tinh took his wife to live on a high peak of Tan Vien mountain. Thuy Tinh also arrived with betrothal gifts later; furious and regretful that he was too late, he summoned clouds and rain, raised the waters to flood the land, and led aquatic creatures in pursuit. The king and Son Tinh stretched iron nets across the upper reaches of the Tu Liem river to block them. Thuy Tinh took another river, from Ly Nhan to the foot of Quang Oai mountain, then followed the banks up to the Hat river estuary, out to the great river, and turned into the Da river to attack Tan Vien. Son Tinh possessed divine powers of transformation; he called [5a] the barbarians to weave bamboo into water barriers, and used crossbows to shoot downwards. (Legend has it that from then on, Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh harbored a generational feud, and every year during the high water season, they often fought each other).

Writing began in late 2009, when singer Skylar Grey resided at the Artula Retreat in Bandon, Oregon,[4] and wrote songs.[5] Later, in New York City, she visited her Universal Music publisher, Jennifer Blakeman, to seek help presenting her work;[5][6] Blakeman suggested she collaborate with Alex da Kid.[5] The producer emailed Grey his track, which suggested a theme of abusive romantic relationships to her as she spontaneously sang lyrics to the melody.[7] She told the Los Angeles Times that she was in an abusive relationship with the music industry: "I love it so much, and I give it all that I have, yet it beats me down."[8] This idea inspired her writing,[8] a process she found came naturally, as if she were creating an alternative pop song for herself.[9] She wrote the chorus to "Love the Way You Lie" in fifteen minutes and recorded vocals for Alex da Kid's demo.[5][10]

question: Describe how the kingdom of Van Lang was organized under the Hung Kings.
answer:
The kingdom of Van Lang, established under the rule of the Hung Kings, was organized through a structured administrative and military framework that reflected both centralized authority and regional governance. At its core, the kingdom was divided into **15 administrative regions**, each serving as a vassal territory under the direct control of Hung Vuong. These regions included notable areas such as **Duong Tuyen**, **Giao Chi**, **Cuu Chan**, and **Cuu Duc**, which were strategically positioned to manage the kingdom’s vast territory. The capital, **Phong Chau** (modern-day Bach Hac district), was designated as the central hub of power, while the remaining regions were governed by appointed officials, ensuring loyalty to the ruling dynasty.

The administrative system relied on a dual hierarchy of **military and civil officials**. **Lac Tuong** (military generals) and **Lac Hau** (civil officials) were appointed by Hung Vuong to oversee governance in each region. This division allowed for efficient management of both defense and domestic affairs. Military generals likely focused on border security and resource control, while civil officials handled taxation, law, and public administration. The king’s sons were designated as **Quan Lang** (royal sons), and daughters as **Mi Nuong**, reinforcing a hereditary system that tied leadership to the royal lineage. Officials themselves followed a hereditary path, with roles passed down through generations as **phu dao**, ensuring continuity in governance.

A unique aspect of Van Lang’s organization was its **cultural and symbolic practices**. The kingdom’s people, facing challenges from water monsters (thuong luong), adopted a custom of **tattooing images of these creatures** onto their bodies. This practice, reportedly initiated by Hung Vuong, served both a practical and symbolic purpose, reflecting the king’s authority to mediate between natural forces and human society. Such rituals underscored the integration of spiritual beliefs into governance, reinforcing the ruler’s role as a mediator between the divine and the populace.

The kingdom’s structure also reflected its **historical context**. The Hong Bang dynasty era, spanning from the reign of Kinh Duong Vuong to the end of the Hung Vuong era, coincided with the 57th year of King Nan of Zhou (258 BC). This timeline highlights the kingdom’s existence during a period of regional fragmentation, as Van Lang’s 15 regions functioned as a defensive buffer against external threats. The division into vassal territories likely served to consolidate power while allowing local autonomy, a balance critical for maintaining stability in a politically fragmented era. Thus, the Van Lang kingdom’s organization was a blend of centralized rule, regional governance, and cultural symbolism, all rooted in the legacy of the Hung Kings.

answer:
The legendary lineage from **Kinh Duong Vuong** to the **first Hung Vuong** is rooted in the foundational myths of the Vietnamese people, which trace the origins of the **Bach Viet** (people of the North) to a divine and heroic lineage. Here's a structured overview:

---

### **1. Kinh Duong Vuong and the Divine Lineage**  
The **Kinh Duong Vuong** (King of the Dragon) is a figure from the **Hung Kings' legend**, which is central to Vietnamese national identity. According to the *Dien Hong* (Red Book) and other ancient texts, the first Hung King, **Hung Vuong Hung Quoc** (Hung King the First), was born from a dragon egg and was the son of **Lao Hoi** (a dragon) and **Mai Co** (a tiger). This divine origin symbolizes the connection between the Vietnamese people and the natural world, with the dragon and tiger representing power and vitality.  

The term **Kinh Duong Vuong** may refer to an earlier ruler or a title for the first Hung King, as the legend often conflates early dynastic figures with mythological ancestors. The lineage of the **Hung Kings** is considered the foundation of the **Bach Viet** people, who are believed to have descended from these divine progenitors.

---

### **2. The First Hung Vuong and the Founding of the Bach Viet**  
The **first Hung Vuong**, **Hung Quoc**, is credited with establishing the first Vietnamese state. According to legend, he ruled from the capital **Phong Chau** (modern-day Phu Tho province) and unified the region through a combination of military prowess and divine favor. His reign marked the beginning of the **Hung Kings' dynasty**, which lasted for 18 generations.  

The **Bach Viet** (literally "people of the North") are said to have originated from this lineage. The term **Bach Viet** contrasts with **Nam Viet** (people of the South), reflecting the division of the region into northern and southern territories. The Hung Kings' rule is depicted as a golden age of cultural and political unity, with the people of the North (Bach Viet) forming the core of the Vietnamese nation.

---

### **3. Mythological Foundations and Cultural Significance**  
The legend of the **Hung Kings** emphasizes themes of **divine right**, **heroism**, and **national unity**. The **dragon and tiger** motifs symbolize the dual forces of creation and protection, while the **dragon egg** birth of Hung Quoc underscores the sacredness of the royal lineage. These myths were later codified in texts like the *Khâm định Việt sử thông giám cương mục* (Compendium of Vietnamese History), which solidified the Hung Kings as the spiritual and historical ancestors of the Vietnamese people.  

The **Bach Viet** identity, rooted in this legend, became a unifying narrative during periods of foreign domination, such as the Chinese dynastic rule. The myth of the Hung Kings provided a sense of continuity and legitimacy, reinforcing the idea that the Vietnamese people were descendants of a noble and divine lineage.

---

### **4. Historical Context and Legacy**  
While the **Hung Kings' legend** is primarily mythological, it has profound historical significance. The **Bach Viet** people, as described in the legend, are often associated with the **Red River Delta** region, which became the heart of Vietnamese civilization. The myth also influenced later dynasties, such as the **Trung Son** (Tay Son) and **Nguyen**, who invoked the legacy of the Hung Kings to legitimize their rule.  

In summary, the legendary line from **Kinh Duong Vuong** to the **first Hung Vuong** represents the mythical origins of the **Bach Viet** people, blending divine ancestry, cultural identity, and historical continuity. This narrative remains a cornerstone of Vietnamese heritage, symbolizing resilience and unity.

answer:
The document associates several legends and customs with the **Hung Vuong era**, a foundational period in Vietnamese history attributed to the legendary Hung Kings. These include:

---

### **1. Tattooing Custom to Repel Water Monsters**  
A key custom tied to the Hung Vuong era is the practice of **tattooing images of water monsters** on the body. According to the text, the king advised people to use ink to tattoo these images, which deterred water monsters from biting or harming them. This custom is linked to the **Bach Viet people** (an ancient Vietnamese group) and is described as originating during the Hung Vuong reign. The practice reflects a blend of **mythological beliefs** and **practical measures** to protect against supernatural threats.

---

### **2. Legend of the Heroic Child (Vu Ninh Hero)**  
A prominent legend recounts the story of a child from **Phu Dong village** who, at a young age, suddenly spoke and offered to defend the kingdom against invaders. The king granted him a sword and horse, and he led the army to victory, defeating enemies at **Vu Ninh mountain**. After the battle, the child ascended to the sky, leaving behind a legacy as a **heavenly general**. A temple was later built in his honor, and he was posthumously titled **Xung Thien Than Vuong** (Heavenly General Vuong). This tale emphasizes **heroism, divine favor, and the supernatural** as themes of the era.

---

### **3. The Myth of Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh**  
The **legend of Son Tinh (Mountain Spirit)** and **Thuy Tinh (Water Spirit)** is central to the Hung Vuong era’s mythology. The story revolves around **Mi Nuong**, the king’s daughter, who married Son Tinh after he outcompeted Thuy Tinh in a betrothal contest. Thuy Tinh, enraged by his defeat, flooded the land to reclaim his wife, leading to a legendary battle. The conflict culminated in Son Tinh using divine powers to block Thuy Tinh’s advances, symbolizing the **eternal rivalry between land and water forces**. This myth underscores **natural elements as deities** and the **struggle for dominance** in Vietnamese cosmology.

---

### **4. Diplomatic and Technological Exchange with the Zhou Dynasty**  
While not a legend, the text mentions a **historical event** during the reign of **King Cheng of Zhou** (1063–1026 BC), where the **Viet people** first visited the Zhou dynasty, offering a white pheasant. The Zhou king ordered the construction of a **south-pointing chariot** to escort the envoys, highlighting **diplomatic relations** and **technological exchange**. This event, though rooted in history, reflects the **cultural and political interactions** of the Hung Vuong era with neighboring regions.

---

### **5. Administrative Structure and Feudal Lords**  
The document also notes that during the Hung Vuong era, the kingdom was divided into **15 regions** governed by feudal lords, with the king’s younger sons assigned to rule them. This administrative practice, while more historical, is presented as a **custom of governance** during the period, emphasizing **centralized authority** and **hereditary leadership**.

---

### **Uncertain or Speculative Elements**  
The text includes **uncertain claims**, such as the idea that **50 children followed their mother to the mountains**, which may reflect oral traditions or later interpretations. These elements lack clear historical evidence and are likely **mythologized or symbolic** rather than factual.

---

In summary, the **Hung Vuong era** is deeply intertwined with **mythological narratives**, **protective customs**, and **historical practices**, reflecting a blend of **spiritual beliefs, heroism, and governance** that shaped early Vietnamese identity.

Kinh Duong Vuong
[1b] His taboo name was Loc Tuc, a descendant of the Than Nong clan.
Year of Nham Tuat, 17th year. In the past, De Minh, the third-generation descendant of Viem De of the Than Nong clan, fathered De Nghi. Later, during a tour of the South, De Minh reached Ngu Linh, married the daughter of Vu Tien, and fathered the king [Kinh Duong Vuong]. The king was a man of sagacious intelligence; De Minh loved him dearly and wanted him to succeed to the throne. The king persistently yielded to his older brother and dared not obey the command. De Minh then established De Nghi as the heir to rule the North, and enfeoffed the king as Kinh Duong Vuong to rule the South, calling it the kingdom of Xich Quy.
The king married the daughter of Dong Dinh Quan named Than Long, and fathered Lac Long Quan (Note: The Tang annals record: during the Kinh Duong period, there was a goat-herding woman who claimed to be the youngest daughter of Dong Dinh Quan; she married the second son of Kinh Xuyen but was abandoned, and wrote a letter asking Lieu Nghi to report this to Dong Dinh Quan. Thus, Kinh Xuyen and Dong Dinh had been allied by marriage for generations).

Lac Long Quan
[2a] His taboo name was Sung Lam, son of Kinh Duong Vuong.
The king married De Lai's daughter, Au Co, and fathered a hundred sons (legend has it she gave birth to a hundred eggs), who are the ancestors of the Bach Viet. One day, the king said to Au Co: "I am of the dragon race, you are of the fairy race; water and fire are incompatible, it is truly difficult for us to be together." They then bid each other farewell, dividing 50 children to follow their mother to the mountains, and 50 children to follow their father to the South (some versions record to the South Sea), and enfeoffed the eldest son as Hung Vuong to succeed the throne.
Historian Ngo Si Lien said: When heaven and earth were first formed, there was a being created from vital energy, which was the Pan Gu clan. From the manifestation of energy came the manifestation of physical forms; nothing exists outside the two energies of yin and yang. The I Ching says: "Heaven and earth intermingle, all things are transformed and purified; male and female unite their essences, all things are born." Therefore, there is husband and wife first, then father and son, and after father and son comes ruler and subject. [2b] However, the birth of sages and worthies is always extraordinary, which is due to the mandate of heaven. Swallowing a dark bird's egg to give birth to the Shang dynasty, stepping on a giant's footprint to establish the Zhou dynasty, are all recorded facts of this nature. The descendant of the Than Nong clan, De Minh, married the daughter of Vu Tien and fathered Kinh Duong Vuong, who is the founding ancestor of the Bach Viet. The king married the daughter of Than Long and fathered Lac Long Quan; Lac Long Quan married the daughter of De Lai and had the auspicious blessing of fathering a hundred sons. Is that not what laid the foundation for our Viet nation's enterprise? Examining the Tongjian Waiji (Comprehensive Mirror, Outer Annals), it states: De Lai was the son of De Nghi; according to that record, Kinh Duong Vuong was the biological younger brother of De Nghi, yet they intermarried; perhaps it was because that era was still primitive and rites and music had not yet been established?

Hung Vuong
[3a] The son of Lac Long Quan (taboo name unknown), established the capital in Phong Chau (now Bach Hac district).
Upon ascending the throne, Hung Vuong set the national name as Van Lang (this country bordered the South Sea to the east, Ba Thuc to the west, Dong Dinh lake to the north, and Ho Ton - which is Champa, now Quang Nam - to the south). He divided the country into 15 administrative regions: Giao Chi, Chu Dien, Vu Ninh, Phuc Loc, Viet Thuong, Ninh Hai, Duong Tuyen, Luc Hai, Vu Dinh, Hoai Hoan, Cuu Chan, Binh Van, Tan Hung, Cuu Duc; all were vassal lands of Hung Vuong; while the region called Van Lang was where the king established the capital. He appointed civil generals called Lac Hau, and military generals called Lac Tuong. The king's sons were called Quan Lang, and daughters were called Mi Nuong. Officials in charge of affairs were called Bo Chinh; their hereditary succession from father to son was called phu dao. Kings of all generations were called Hung Vuong. At that time, the people living in the forests and mountains saw that the rivers and streams had shrimp and fish, so they invited each other to catch fish for food, but were often harmed by water monsters (thuong luong). [3b] They came to report this to the king. The king said: "The barbarians in the mountains are different from aquatic species; those aquatic species favor their own kind and hate other species, which is why you are harmed by them." The king then told everyone to use ink to tattoo images of water monsters on their bodies. From then on, the water monsters saw them and no longer bit or harmed them. The tattooing custom of the Bach Viet people probably started from there.

2,	"Quang Trung (Chinese characters: 光中, 1753 – September 16, 1792), whose pre-coronation title was Bac Binh Vuong (北平王 - Prince of Northern Peace), birth name Ho Thom (胡𦹳), originally from Nghe An and later renamed Nguyen Hue (阮惠), was a Vietnamese politician and military leader. He was the 2nd emperor of the Tay Son Dynasty after his older brother, Emperor Thai Duc Nguyen Nhac, abdicated and passed the throne to him.

Nguyen Hue and his two brothers, known as the Tay Son heroes (Tây Sơn tam kiệt), were the leaders of the Tay Son uprising that ended the Trinh–Nguyen civil war between the two feudal groups of Trinh in the north and Nguyen in the south, overthrowing these two groups along with the Later Le Dynasty, ending the division of Dang Trong (Inner Realm) and Dang Ngoai (Outer Realm) that lasted for 2 centuries. In addition, Quang Trung was also the one who defeated the invasions of Dai Viet by Siam from the south and the Great Qing from the north. He personally commanded troops from the age of 18, and over 20 consecutive years, he fought in dozens of major battles without losing a single one.

Historian Phan Huy Le evaluated that "Quang Trung was not only a brilliant military leader but also a politician with exceptional talent"[1]. With a progressive vision, in just 3 years, he successively proposed many progressive reform plans in economics, culture, education, military,... to build the country and absorb modern science and technology from the West.[2] Regarding personnel, he issued an edict seeking talented people and heavily utilized many talents such as Ngo Thi Nham, Phan Huy Ich, Nguyen Thiep, Nguyen Huy Luong,... In terms of the military, he built an army equipped with modern weapons. Economically, he reformed the taxation and land systems, encouraged handicrafts, and expanded foreign trade with the West. Regarding education, he improved the examination system in a practical direction, promulgated policies to encourage learning, encouraged the use of pure Vietnamese Nom script instead of Han script, reorganized redundant temples, and eradicated superstitions. Historians highly appreciate these reforms because they had a very progressive tendency, surpassing contemporary Asian countries, and could bring the country out of the stagnation that had lasted over 100 years under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system. Even much later (1822), overseas Chinese who lived in Hue under the Tay Son era still reminisced about Nguyen Hue's rule; they commented to a British merchant that Quang Trung ruled more mildly and fairly than the Nguyen dynasty kings (Gia Long and Minh Mang)[3] (see details at progressive reforms of King Quang Trung).

The active life of Nguyen Hue made a decisive contribution to the cause of national reunification of the Tay Son dynasty[4]. After 20 years of continuous warfare and 3 years of ruling the country, when the country's situation began to show positive changes, Quang Trung died suddenly at the age of 39. After his death, the Tay Son Dynasty weakened rapidly. His successor, Quang Toan, was still too young (9 years old) to lead Dai Viet; the royal court fell into internal conflict and failed to continue resisting Nguyen Anh.

Nguyen Hue is listed by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism as one of the 14 typical national heroes of Vietnam.[5] Many schools and streets in localities are named Quang Trung and Nguyen Hue.

According to the books Khâm định Việt sử Thông giám cương mục and Đại Nam thực lục: Nguyen Hue's ancestors were from Hung Nguyen district, Nghe An region. Around the Thinh Duc years (reign name of Le Than Tong) (1653–1657), they were captured by Lord Nguyen's army and brought back to live in Tuy Vien district, Hoai Nhon prefecture. Several generations later, Nguyen Nhac held the position of a minor clerk (Biện lại) at the Van Don tollgate. The book Việt Nam sử lược adds: Nguyen Hue's father, Ho Phi Phuc, moved his home to Kien Thanh hamlet, and had 3 children: the eldest was Nhac, the second was Hue, and the third was Lu.[6][7] His mother was Nguyen Thi Dong.

According to the book Lịch sử nội chiến Việt Nam từ 1771 đến 1802 (History of the Vietnamese Civil War from 1771 to 1802), the ancestors of the Tay Son family originally bore the surname Ho in Huong Cai village, Hung Nguyen district, Nghe An province, descending from Ho Quy Ly,[8] and followed Lord Nguyen to settle in the South when Lord Nguyen crossed the Thay Wall to attack the Le–Trinh territory reaching Nghe An (in 1655). ### **Military Achievements of Quang Trung**  
Quang Trung, also known as Nguyen Hue, was a formidable military leader whose campaigns significantly shaped the history of Vietnam. He began commanding troops at the age of 18 and led over 20 years of continuous warfare, achieving victory in dozens of major battles without a single loss. His most notable military feats include repelling the invasions of the Kingdom of Siam from the south and the Qing Dynasty from the north. These victories not only secured the survival of the Tay Son dynasty but also demonstrated his strategic brilliance and tactical prowess. His leadership during the prolonged conflict between the Trinh and Nguyen feudal factions further solidified his reputation as a unifying force for the nation. The document emphasizes that his military campaigns were instrumental in the Tay Son dynasty’s national reunification efforts, which culminated in the end of the 200-year division between the Trinh and Nguyen regimes.  

### **Political Reforms and Governance**  
Beyond his military successes, Quang Trung implemented sweeping political and administrative reforms to modernize and stabilize the country. Within three years of ascending to power, he introduced progressive policies across economics, culture, education, and military affairs. Key reforms included modernizing the armed forces with Western technology, reorganizing taxation and land systems to reduce exploitation, and promoting handicrafts and foreign trade to boost the economy. In education, he reformed the examination system to prioritize practical knowledge, encouraged the use of the Vietnamese Nom script over the traditional Han script, and abolished superstitious practices by reorganizing redundant temples. His efforts to attract and utilize talented individuals, such as Ngo Thi Nham and Phan Huy Ich, further strengthened his governance. Historians highlight these reforms as remarkably progressive, surpassing contemporary Asian nations and revitalizing a country that had stagnated under the Trinh–Nguyen feudal system for over a century.  

### **Legacy and Impact**  
Quang Trung’s legacy endures through his dual contributions to military and political development. His ability to unify the nation through warfare and governance is celebrated as a turning point in Vietnamese history. Even after his untimely death at 39, his reforms and leadership left a lasting impact, with later generations, including overseas Chinese communities, recalling his fair and just rule in contrast to the later Nguyen dynasty. The document underscores his role as both a brilliant military strategist and a visionary reformer, whose policies laid the groundwork for Vietnam’s eventual modernization. His recognition as one of Vietnam’s 14 national heroes by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism further attests to his enduring significance in the nation’s historical narrative.
